name: Gonin-Kan
description: Gonin-Kan (äº”äººã‚«ãƒ³ - 'Five People Kan') is the most popular variation of Kan, a Japanese trick-taking game from Aomori prefecture. Played by 5-6 players using a 50-card deck (standard 52 minus three 2s plus joker). Features unique partnership formation each round based on joker and trump ace holders, with the kankei (partners) against the mukankei (non-partners).

history.origins:
Country/Region of Origin: Japan (Aomori Prefecture)
Time Period: Early-to-mid 20th century
Creator(s): Japanese regional game (folk origin)
Etymology: 'Gonin-Kan' means 'Five People Kan'; 'Kan' is the generic name, also called 'Etori' (picture taking)
timeline: Early 20th Century: Kan game family develops in Aomori prefecture
Mid 20th Century: Gonin-Kan emerges as the most popular variation
Regional Development: Game particularly popular in Goshogawara and Tsugaru
Modern Era: Tournament play established with standardized rules
Present Day: Remains popular in Aomori; other variations include Yonin-Kan (4-player) and Gambari-Kan (3-player)
history.cultural: Kan represents a significant part of regional Japanese card gaming culture in Aomori prefecture. The game is distinct from the more widely known Hanafuda and standard playing card games of Japan. Tournament play has helped standardize rules, though informal games may have local variations.
history.evolution: Kan is a family of games with many variations. Gonin-Kan (5-player) became the most popular form, though 4-player (Yonin-Kan/Damari-Kan) and 3-player (Gambari-Kan) versions exist. Related games include Kakeya Toranpu and other Etori (picture-taking) games.

rules.objective: The kankei (partnership of joker holder and trump ace holder) tries to win more than 8 of the 16 available points (ace, king, queen, jack of each suit). The mukankei (other players) try to prevent this.
rules.gameplay:
ROUND STRUCTURE:
- Round = 1-3 successive deals by same dealer (maki-yaku)
- Round ends when kankei loses a deal or wins 3 successive deals
- New dealer is player to right of previous dealer FIRST DEAL OF ROUND:
1. Trump suit determined by round number (clubs, diamonds, hearts rotating; spades for final round 'Tome-Suppe')
2. Dealer deals 10 cards each
3. Joker holder and trump ace holder declare 'kan' and become partners (kankei)
4. If same player holds both, they partner with player two places to their right
5. Partners must not sit adjacent; exchange seats if necessary
6. Partners exchange information by showing cards PLAY:
1. Kankei decides who leads first ('Iku' = I lead, 'Koi' = You lead)
2. Must follow suit if possible; joker can be played to any trick (except first and last)
3. Joker always wins trick; if no joker, highest trump wins; if no trump, highest of led suit wins
4. Joker holder cannot be forced to play joker until 9th trick (odori ban)
keyRules: Partnerships change each round based on card holdings
Joker is always highest but cannot be played in first or last trick
Partners cannot sit adjacent; must exchange seats if randomly seated together
Trump suit rotates: clubs, diamonds, hearts (spades for final round)
Kankei must win more than 8 points to succeed
Joker holder leads the trump suit when playing joker

strategy.basic:
For Beginners:
1. Learn the 16 point cards (A, K, Q, J of each suit)
2. If you're kankei, coordinate with your partner through the card exchange
3. Save the joker for critical tricks (but must play it in 9th trick)
4. Count points taken to know if you're on track
strategy.intermediate:
1. Track which point cards have been played
2. As mukankei, cooperate with other non-partners to stop kankei
3. Use the seat exchange rule to your advantage
4. Calculate whether kankei can reach 9+ points based on visible cards
strategy.advanced:
1. Complex probability of joker location based on bidding
2. Optimal card exchange strategies for partners
3. Bluffing by bidding behavior
4. Endgame calculation for exact point distribution
5. Tournament scoring optimization over multiple rounds
tips: The joker is extremely powerful - use it wisely
Communication with your partner is limited to the card exchange - make it count
Watch for sukonku (9-7) situations which have special scoring
The final round with spades trumps (Tome-Suppe) can be decisive
